## Appendix A Estimates for the Poisson Equation with Drift

In this section, we discuss the Poisson equation with constant drift $b=Ue_{1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle b\cdot\nabla\theta-\Delta\theta=f+\operatorname{div}g. $$

We find the fundamental solution and derive $\mathrm{L}^{p}$ estimates.

### A.1 The Fundamental Solution

We first find the fundamental solution to Equation (37) in three dimensions.

#### Lemma A.1.

The fundamental solution $\Gamma$ that solves $b\cdot\nabla\Gamma-\Delta\Gamma=\delta_{0}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi r}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(r-x_{1})},\qquad\lambda=\frac{U}{2}. $$

Here $x=(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})$ , $b=Ue_{1}$ , $r=|x|$ , and $U\geq 0$ .

#### Proof.

To verify its validity, we first compute away from $r=0$ the gradient $\nabla\Gamma=\Gamma\nabla\log\Gamma$ with

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\log\Gamma \displaystyle=-\nabla\log r-\lambda\nabla(r-x_{1})=-\frac{\hat{x}}{r}-\lambda(\hat{x}-e_{1})=-\frac{1}{r}\hat{x}-\lambda\hat{x}+\lambda e_{1}. $$

Here we used the notation $\hat{x}=x/r$ . Next we compute the Laplacian:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\Gamma \displaystyle=\operatorname{div}\nabla\Gamma=\operatorname{div}(\Gamma\nabla\log\Gamma)=\Gamma|\nabla\log\Gamma|^{2}+\Gamma\Delta\log\Gamma, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\log\Gamma=\operatorname{div}\left(-\frac{1}{r}\hat{x}-\lambda\hat{x}\right)=-\left(\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\right)\frac{2}{r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}=-\left(\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\right)^{2}+\lambda^{2}. $$

Substituting this into $\Delta\Gamma$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\log\Gamma|^{2}+\Delta\log\Gamma \displaystyle=\left|\left(\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\right)\hat{x}-\lambda e_{1}\right|^{2}-\left(\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\right)^{2}+\lambda^{2} \displaystyle=-2\lambda e_{1}\cdot\left(\left(\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\right)\hat{x}-\lambda e_{1}\right)=2\lambda e_{1}\cdot\nabla\log\Gamma. $$

Hence, $\Delta\Gamma=(2\lambda e_{1}\cdot\nabla\log\Gamma)\Gamma=Ue_{1}\cdot\nabla\Gamma=b\cdot\nabla\Gamma$ .

We have verified that $b\cdot\nabla\Gamma-\Delta\Gamma=0$ in the open set $\mathbb{R}^{3}\setminus\{0\}$ . It remains to check the behavior near $r=0$ . Taking a smooth test function $\varphi$ supported in $B_{r}$ , we compute

$$ \displaystyle\int_{B_{r}}(b\cdot\nabla\Gamma-\Delta\Gamma)\varphi\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}x \displaystyle=\int_{B_{r}}(-b\cdot\nabla\varphi-\Delta\varphi)\Gamma\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}x \displaystyle\qquad+\int_{\partial B_{r}}(\Gamma b-\varphi\nabla\Gamma+\Gamma\nabla\varphi)\cdot n\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma. $$

Fixing $\varphi$ , the left-hand side is independent on the value of $r$ , so we may let $r\to 0$ . We notice that $\Gamma$ has the following trivial bound:

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma(x)|\leq\frac{1}{4\pi r}. $$

All the integrals on the right-hand-side except the one with $\nabla\Gamma$ will vanish as $r\to 0$ . Moreover,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\partial B_{r}}\nabla\Gamma\cdot\varphi n\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma=\int_{\partial B_{r}}\Gamma\nabla\log\Gamma\cdot\varphi n\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma=-\int_{\partial B_{r}}\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{r}\hat{x}+\lambda\hat{x}-\lambda e_{1}\right)\cdot\varphi n\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma. $$

Only the term with $\frac{1}{r}$ will survive in the limit $r\to 0$ . Note that $n=\hat{x}$ , so we have

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{r\to 0}\int_{\partial B_{r}}(-\nabla\Gamma)\cdot\varphi n\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma=\lim_{r\to 0}\int_{\partial B_{r}}\frac{\Gamma}{r}\varphi\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\sigma=\varphi(0). $$

This finishes the proof. ∎

From the form of the fundamental solution, we see immediately that $|\Gamma|\leq\frac{1}{r}$ and $\Gamma\in\mathrm{L}^{3,\infty}$ . We would like to establish an upper bound for $|\nabla\Gamma|$ that is uniform in the size of $\lambda$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle|r(\hat{x}-e_{1})|^{2}=(x_{1}-r)^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}=(r-x_{1})^{2}+r^{2}-x_{1}^{2}=2r(r-x_{1}). $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\log\Gamma|\leq\frac{1}{r}+\lambda\sqrt{\frac{2(r-x_{1})}{r}}\leq(\lambda(r-x_{1})+1)\sqrt{\frac{2}{r(r-x_{1})}}. $$

We used the inequality $0\leq r-x_{1}\leq 2r$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\Gamma|\leq\frac{1}{4\pi r}\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(r-x_{1})}(\lambda(r-x_{1})+1)\sqrt{\frac{2}{r(r-x_{1})}}\leq Cr^{-\frac{3}{2}}(r-x_{1})^{-\frac{1}{2}}. $$

We used that $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(r-x_{1})}(1+\lambda(r-x_{1}))$ is bounded uniformly in $x_{1}$ , $r$ , and $\lambda$ .

#### Lemma A.2.

$\nabla\Gamma$ is bounded in $\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2},\infty}_{x_{1}}\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x_{2},x_{3}}$ uniformly in $\lambda$ .

#### Proof.

By direct integration:

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}} \displaystyle\left[r^{-\frac{3}{2}}(r-x_{1})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}x_{2}\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}x_{3} \displaystyle=2\pi\int_{0}^{\infty}(\rho^{2}+x_{1}^{2})^{-\frac{9}{8}}\left[(\rho^{2}+x_{1}^{2})^{\frac{1}{2}}-x_{1}\right]^{-\frac{3}{4}}\rho\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}\rho\leq\frac{4}{|x_{1}|}. $$

Since $\frac{1}{x_{1}}\in\mathrm{L}^{1,\infty}_{x_{1}}$ , we conclude that $\nabla\Gamma\in\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2},\infty}_{x_{1}}\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x_{2},x_{3}}$ . ∎

### A.2 Local $\mathrm{L}^{p}$ Estimates

We have found $\Gamma\in\mathrm{L}^{3,\infty}$ and $\nabla\Gamma\in\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2},\infty}_{x_{1}}\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2}}_{x_{2},x_{3}}$ , with bounds uniform in the size of the drift. Therefore, if $f\in\mathrm{L}^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , $1<p<\frac{3}{2}$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Gamma*f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}}\lesssim\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{p}} $$

with $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{2}{3}$ . If $g\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})$ , $1<q<3$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Gamma*\operatorname{div}g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}}\lesssim\left\|g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}} $$

with $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{3}$ . A proof of these convolution inequalities is given in [5].

Recall $b=Ue_{1}$ . Suppose $\theta$ solves Equation (37) in a capsule $\mathcal{C}$ of radius $R$ , length $L\geq R$ . We want to derive a local estimate on $\theta$ .

#### Lemma A.3.

If $\theta\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})$ solves Equation (37) in $\mathcal{C}$ with $f,g\in\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})$ for some $1<q<3$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\theta\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}(\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{C})}\lesssim R\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\left\|g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\left(\frac{UR}{L}+\frac{1}{R}\right)\left\|\theta\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}:=\operatorname{RHS}, $$

where $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{q}-\frac{1}{3}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix a non-negative cut-off function $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathcal{C})$ with $\phi\equiv 1$ inside $\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{C}$ , satisfying bounds as in Equation (14). Then

$$ \displaystyle b\cdot\nabla(\phi\theta)-\Delta(\phi\theta)=\phi f+\operatorname{div}(\phi g)+\theta b\cdot\nabla\phi-2\operatorname{div}(\theta\nabla\phi)+\theta\Delta\phi-g\cdot\nabla\phi. $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{f} \displaystyle=\phi f+\theta b\cdot\nabla\phi+\theta\Delta\phi-g\cdot\nabla\phi, \displaystyle\tilde{g} \displaystyle=\phi g-2\theta\nabla\phi. $$

Then $\phi\theta$ solves

$$ \displaystyle b\cdot\nabla(\phi\theta)-\Delta(\phi\theta)=\tilde{f}+\operatorname{div}\tilde{g}. $$

The function $\phi\theta$ is the unique compactly supported solution, so $\phi\theta=\Gamma*(\tilde{f}+\operatorname{div}\tilde{g})$ . First, for the forcing term in divergence form, we note that

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\tilde{g}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}\lesssim\left\|g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\frac{1}{R}\left\|\theta\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}\leq\text{RHS}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Gamma*\operatorname{div}\tilde{g}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}(\mathcal{C})}\lesssim\left\|\tilde{g}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}\lesssim\text{RHS}. $$

For the forcing term not in divergence form, we notice that

$$ \displaystyle\|{\tilde{f}}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{3})} \displaystyle\lesssim\left\|f\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\frac{1}{R}\left\|g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\left(\frac{U}{L}+\frac{1}{R^{2}}\right)\left\|\theta\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}. $$

Here we used that $|b\cdot\nabla\phi|\lesssim\frac{U}{L}$ . Moreover, we have the elementary bound:

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Gamma\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2}}(3\mathcal{C})}^{\frac{3}{2}}\lesssim\int_{3\mathcal{C}}\frac{1}{r^{\frac{3}{2}}}\mathop{\kern 0.0pt\mathrm{d}}\!{}x\leq CR^{\frac{3}{2}}, $$

where the constant $C$ does not depend on $L$ . Suppose $\tilde{\Gamma}=\phi_{1}\Gamma$ , where $\phi_{1}$ is a smooth function supported on $2\mathcal{C}$ and vanishing off $3\mathcal{C}$ . Since $\tilde{f}$ is supported in $\mathcal{C}$ , we have that $(\tilde{\Gamma}\ast\tilde{f})(x)=(\Gamma\ast\tilde{f})(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal{C}$ . In addition, we have by Young’s convolution inequality:

$$ \displaystyle\left\|\Gamma*\tilde{f}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}(\mathcal{C})}=\left\|\tilde{\Gamma}*\tilde{f}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}(\mathcal{C})} \displaystyle\leq\left\|\tilde{\Gamma}*\tilde{f}\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{r}(\mathbb{R}^{3})}\leq\left\|\Gamma\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{\frac{3}{2}}(3\mathcal{C})}\|\tilde{f}\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})} \displaystyle\lesssim R\|f\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\left\|g\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}+\left(\frac{UR}{L}+\frac{1}{R}\right)\left\|\theta\right\|_{\mathrm{L}^{q}(\mathcal{C})}. $$

Since $\phi\equiv 1$ in $\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{C}$ , we have completed the proof. ∎
